why: Pain and emotional well-being can affect one another. Supporting either may make recovery easier to navigate, even when symptoms do not immediately change.

slides.title: A Two-Way Relationship
slides.content: Living with pain can affect mood, sleep, relationships, and stress. Those experiences can also influence symptoms and participation.

slides.title: Your Pain Is Still Real
slides.content: An emotional influence does not mean pain is imaginary or ‘all in your head.’ Whole-person care considers both physical and psychosocial factors.

slides.title: Skills Can Help
slides.content: CBT, ACT, pacing, relaxation, and social support may help some people reduce distress or improve participation. Effects vary and none is a guaranteed pain reliever.

slides.title: Choose Support Early
slides.content: Speak with a qualified professional if anxiety, low mood, trauma, or hopelessness is persistent, worsening, or interfering with daily life.

slides.title: Try One Grounding Step
slides.content: Name what you are feeling, notice one thing around you, and choose one manageable next action. Stop any exercise that feels unhelpful.

title: Name the emotion, then choose the action
